title: The farewell tawaf
hook: a last circling before leaving Mecca

segments.voice: Yesterday, the days of tashriq in Mina, and your line: eat and remember. Did one meal get your full attention, from the first bite? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-eight.

People are already leaving. The rites are done, the days at Mina are over, and pilgrims are heading off in every direction, home to wherever home is. Ibn Abbas remembers the moment. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ stops them with a sentence: none of you should leave until the last thing you do is at the House. Not the last purchase, not the last meal. The House. So before the road home, there's one more walk around the Ka'ba. Today, the farewell tawaf.
screen: `LEAVING IN EVERY DIRECTION.` → `NONE OF YOU SHOULD LEAVE…` → `…UNTIL THE LAST THING IS THE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: First, the rule. The report from Ibn Abbas, in Sahih Muslim, is simple: let the last of your time be at the House. A pilgrim's stay ends where it began, circling the Ka'ba. Second, the exception. In another report from Ibn Abbas, in Sahih al-Bukhari, people were commanded to make their last act at the House, except that it was lightened for a woman on her period. She may set out without it. Two days ago, Safiyyah's story showed which circling couldn't be skipped. This is the one that could be lifted. Third, how the schools weigh it. Some schools of law hold the farewell tawaf to be required of pilgrims leaving Mecca, so that missing it calls for an offering. Others hold it to be strongly recommended. Each school reads the same reports, and each has its reasons. Fourth, the word itself. Wada' means a farewell. Tradition calls the Prophet's own pilgrimage, the one these lessons have been following, the Farewell Pilgrimage, Hajjat al-Wada', and he did not make another. So there are two goodbyes folded together here: a pilgrim's goodbye to the House, and the memory of the Prophet's goodbye to his people. What the rite teaches is a way of leaving. Not slipping out the side door. Not letting the last memory be a crowded shop or a line for the bus. Going back to the center, once more, and leaving from there, with the place you're leaving as the last thing you saw.
screen: `LET THE LAST OF IT BE AT THE HOUSE.` · `LIGHTENED FOR A WOMAN ON HER PERIOD.` · `REQUIRED, OR STRONGLY RECOMMENDED.` · `WADA': A FAREWELL.` · then, large: `GOODBYE TO THE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: The practice: say goodbye well. Settle, and breathe. Think of a goodbye that's coming. The end of a job, a friend moving, a child leaving for school, a visit with a parent that ends on Sunday. Or think of a goodbye you rushed, one that ended in a parking lot or a text. How would you want the last moment to go? Who would you look at? What would you say? Let the picture form slowly. If you pray, you can hold that person in your du'a. If you don't, simply hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.
The farewell tawaf. The last circling of the Ka'ba before a pilgrim leaves Mecca, so the final act of the journey is at the House. Today's word.

Your line: goodbye to the house. Today, when you leave a place or a person, don't slip away. Turn, look, and say goodbye on purpose. Tomorrow: visiting Medina. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Before leaving Mecca, pilgrims circle the Ka'ba one last time in the farewell tawaf; women on their period are excused from it, and the schools differ on whether it is required or strongly recommended.

notes: Muslim 1327 (Ibn Abbas): people leaving in every direction; 'none of you should depart until his last act is at the House'. Confirm.
Bukhari 1755 (Ibn Abbas; also Muslim 1328): commanded, lightened for the menstruating woman. Confirm.

Schools: Hanafi, Shafi'i (dominant view) and Hanbali hold tawaf al-wada' wajib with dam if missed; Maliki holds it sunnah. A general fiqh claim not in the cited texts; confirm the summary and whether to mention the Shafi'i minority view.
'Hajjat al-Wada'... because he did not live to make another' is attributed to tradition; confirm phrasing.
